es: Deducir por el contexto el significado de modismos habituales de deporte, cocina y dinero en conversaciones reales.

the ball is in your court

vocabulary.en: have your cake and eat it
vocabulary.es: querer todas las ventajas a la vez

teaching.en: It is an idiom, so nobody expected the manager to mean a real page when she said we all need to be on the same page.
teaching.es: Es un modismo, así que nadie esperaba que la gerente se refiriera a una página real cuando dijo que todos debemos estar en la misma página.
teaching.explanationEs: On the same page: todos tienen la misma información y están de acuerdo; no habla de páginas.
segments: It is an idiom, so nobody expected the manager to mean a real
page when she said we all need to be on the same page.
teaching.audioText: It is an idiom, so nobody expected the manager to mean a real page when she said we all need to be on the same page.

teaching.en: The client rejected our design, so we are back to square one and have to find a completely new idea for the launch.
teaching.es: El cliente rechazó nuestro diseño, así que volvemos a empezar y tenemos que encontrar una idea completamente nueva para el lanzamiento.
teaching.explanationEs: Back to square one: viene de los juegos de mesa; significa volver al punto de partida.
segments: The client rejected our design, so we are back to square one
and have to find a completely new idea for the launch.
teaching.audioText: The client rejected our design, so we are back to square one and have to find a completely new idea for the launch.

teaching.en: I have sent you my offer, so now the ball is in your court, and I will wait for your answer before I do anything else.
teaching.es: Te he enviado mi oferta, así que ahora te toca a ti, y esperaré tu respuesta antes de hacer nada más.
teaching.explanationEs: The ball is in your court viene del tenis: la siguiente jugada le corresponde a la otra persona.
segments: I have sent you my offer, so now the ball is in your
court, and I will wait for your answer before I do anything else.
teaching.audioText: I have sent you my offer, so now the ball is in your court, and I will wait for your answer before I do anything else.

teaching.en: The garden project is on the back burner until spring, because we have no money for it and every other task is more urgent.
teaching.es: El proyecto del jardín está en pausa hasta la primavera, porque no tenemos dinero para él y cualquier otra tarea es más urgente.
teaching.explanationEs: On the back burner: como una olla en el fondo de la cocina, se atiende más tarde.
segments: The garden project is on the back burner until spring, because we
have no money for it and every other task is more urgent.
teaching.audioText: The garden project is on the back burner until spring, because we have no money for it and every other task is more urgent.

teaching.en: Here is an idiom about money: a weekend in Paris will not break the bank if we book early, but do not bank on cheap flights in August.
teaching.es: Aquí tienes un modismo sobre dinero: un fin de semana en París no arruinará el presupuesto si reservamos pronto, pero no cuentes con vuelos baratos en agosto.
teaching.explanationEs: Break the bank: costar demasiado; con not significa que es asequible. Bank on: contar con algo.
segments: Here is an idiom about money: a weekend in Paris will not break the
bank if we book early, but do not bank on cheap flights in August.
teaching.audioText: Here is an idiom about money: a weekend in Paris will not break the bank if we book early, but do not bank on cheap flights in August.

teaching.en: Another idiom: you cannot have your cake and eat it, so once the exam is over, turn the page and start planning the next one.
teaching.es: Otro modismo: no puedes tenerlo todo a la vez, así que cuando termine el examen, pasa página y empieza a planear el siguiente.
teaching.explanationEs: Have your cake and eat it: querer dos cosas incompatibles. Turn the page: dejar atrás lo que pasó.
segments: Another idiom: you cannot have your cake and eat it, so once the
exam is over, turn the page and start planning the next one.
teaching.audioText: Another idiom: you cannot have your cake and eat it, so once the exam is over, turn the page and start planning the next one.

prompt.es: Deduce el sentido de «back to square one» por el contexto.

choices.text: We had to return to the place where we began.
We had to start planning again from the beginning.
We had to go back to the last stage of a game.

feedback.es: La pista es que hay que elegir de nuevo lugar, fecha y menú: el plan vuelve al punto de partida.

hint.es: Fíjate en todo lo que hay que decidir otra vez al final del texto.

origin.text: We planned a picnic for Saturday, but it rained all morning and the park was under water. By noon Ana said we had to choose a new place, a new date and a new menu, so we were back to square one.

prompt.es: Completa: «Tom convocó una reunión para que todos estuvieran en la misma página.»

answer.text: page

feedback.es: On the same page significa compartir la misma información y estar de acuerdo; aquí el equipo tenía dos fechas distintas.

hint.es: Es lo que se comparte cuando todos leen lo mismo.

origin.text: Half the team thought the deadline was Friday; the other half thought it was Monday. Before the launch, Tom called a short meeting to make sure everyone was on the same ___.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Envié mi oferta, así que ahora te toca a ti.»

answer.text: I sent my offer so the ball is in your court

feedback.es: La estructura the ball is in your court marca que la siguiente jugada es de la otra persona; so introduce la consecuencia.

hint.es: Empieza con I sent y termina con your court.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada modismo con su significado.

feedback.es: Cada modismo tiene un sentido figurado que no sale de sus palabras: pausa, coste excesivo, facilidad y reinicio.

prompt.es: Escucha la conversación y elige qué deciden sobre la banda en directo.

choices.text: They will drop the band idea for good because it costs too much.
They will book a cheaper band to play at the picnic on Friday.
They will postpone the band until the following year.

feedback.es: «Put on the back burner until next year» significa aplazarlo: la banda queda para el año próximo, no se cancela ni se contrata ahora.

origin.audio: Two colleagues were planning the office party. One said the budget was tight, so a big dinner would break the bank. The other suggested a picnic in the park, which would be a piece of cake to organise. They agreed to put the idea of a live band on the back burner until next year, and before leaving, the first one made sure they were on the same page: picnic, Friday, everyone brings their own drinks.

prompt.es: Con la misma conversación, ¿qué piensa uno de los colegas del picnic?

choices.text: That it will be easy to organise and suits the tight budget.
That it will be simple to organise but too informal for an office party.
That it will be cheap but very demanding for the team to organise.

feedback.es: «A piece of cake» significa algo muy fácil, y el picnic se propone precisamente como alternativa barata a la cena.

origin.audio: Two colleagues were planning the office party. One said the budget was tight, so a big dinner would break the bank. The other suggested a picnic in the park, which would be a piece of cake to organise. They agreed to put the idea of a live band on the back burner until next year, and before leaving, the first one made sure they were on the same page: picnic, Friday, everyone brings their own drinks.

prompt.es: Lee la nota. ¿Qué deja entender el entrenador sobre la capitana?

choices.text: That he is avoiding responsibility and expects her to take the blame.
That she must make the decision and that he trusts her judgement.
That he doubts her judgement and will change her plan on Saturday.

feedback.es: «The ball is in your court» traslada la decisión a la capitana, y añade que ella conoce mejor al equipo: le da su confianza.

origin.text: Coach's note: “I have given you three plans for Saturday's match. I am not going to choose for you, because you know the team better than I do. Now the ball is in your court, captain.”

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué actitud transmite el hablante hacia el examen.

choices.text: He is sure she will pass, so she need not worry about anything on the day.
He believes the examiner will make the test easy for her this time.
He is confident in her but reminds her not to rely on luck.

feedback.es: «A piece of cake» expresa confianza en su preparación; «do not bank on a perfect day» añade una advertencia: no hay que contar solo con la suerte.

origin.audio: Don't stress about the driving test. You have practised every evening for two months, and the examiner is known to be friendly. For you, it will be a piece of cake. Still, do not bank on a perfect day: worry can appear even when you have prepared well.

prompt.es: Completa: «Un concierto grande arruinaría el presupuesto.»

answer.text: break

feedback.es: Break the bank es costar más de lo que se tiene; el contexto indica que el presupuesto apenas alcanza para libros.

origin.text: The school wanted a big concert with a famous band, but the whole budget for the year is barely enough for new books. A big concert would simply ___ the bank.

prompt.es: Según Leo, ¿qué necesitan hacer Mia y él antes de avisar a todos?

choices.text: Agree on one shared version of the facts.
Move the party to a day that suits them both.
Ask everyone else which date they prefer.

feedback.es: Get on the same page es ponerse de acuerdo sobre lo mismo: antes de informar, ambos deben compartir una versión de los hechos.

origin.text: Mia thought the party was on Friday; Leo was sure it was on Saturday. They checked the invitation twice and found two different dates. Leo said: “We need to get on the same page before we tell everyone.”

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué opina el segundo vecino sobre el futuro.

choices.text: He is angry and thinks the other neighbour should apologise again.
He is hopeful but cautious, since he expects the change to be slow.
He is sure that the noise will stop as soon as they shake hands.

feedback.es: Acepta pasar página, pero «could not bank on a quick change» muestra cautela: espera un cambio lento.

origin.audio: After months of arguments, the two neighbours finally said sorry to each other. It is time to turn the page, said one of them. The other nodded, but he admitted that he could not bank on a quick change. He hoped, though, that this time they would not both try to have their cake and eat it, asking for silence from the other side while playing loud music themselves.

prompt.es: Completa: «El jefe rechazó nuestro plan y volvimos a empezar de cero.»

answer.text: square

feedback.es: Back to square one describe volver al principio tras un intento fallido; square va seguido de one.

origin.text: The manager refused our plan, and none of the ideas can be reused. After weeks of work, we are back to ___ one.

prompt.es: Ordena: «No arruinará el presupuesto si vamos juntos.»

answer.text: It will not break the bank if we go together
accepted: It will not break the bank if we go together
It won't break the bank if we go together

feedback.es: La parte fija es break the bank: solo se adapta el auxiliar will not y el resto de la frase.

es: Usar modismos con la gramática correcta: adaptar tiempo y persona del verbo sin cambiar la parte fija.

usesVocabulary: hit the nail on the head
cost an arm and a leg

vocabulary.es: librarse por los pelos de un peligro
superar una crisis, capear el temporal

vocabulary.en: hit the nail on the head
cost an arm and a leg
vocabulary.es: costar un ojo de la cara

teaching.en: Sara spilled the beans about the surprise party, although she had promised to keep the secret until Friday.
teaching.es: Sara reveló el secreto de la fiesta sorpresa, aunque había prometido guardarlo hasta el viernes.
teaching.explanationEs: Spill the beans: el verbo cambia (spilled) pero the beans no cambia.
segments: Sara spilled the beans about the surprise party, although
she had promised to keep the secret until Friday.
teaching.audioText: Sara spilled the beans about the surprise party, although she had promised to keep the secret until Friday.

teaching.en: A crown can cost an arm and a leg, so I bit the bullet and booked it early, and I dodged a bullet when the tooth got no worse.
teaching.es: Una corona puede costar un ojo de la cara, así que me aguanté y reservé pronto, y me libré por los pelos cuando la muela no empeoró.
teaching.explanationEs: Cost an arm and a leg, bite the bullet (bit) y dodge a bullet (dodged): solo cambia el verbo.
segments: A crown can cost an arm and a leg, so I bit the bullet and
booked it early, and I dodged a bullet when the tooth got no worse.
teaching.audioText: A crown can cost an arm and a leg, so I bit the bullet and booked it early, and I dodged a bullet when the tooth got no worse.

teaching.en: You hit the nail on the head: that is exactly the problem, and we would have missed it without your report.
teaching.es: Diste en el clavo: ese es exactamente el problema, y lo habríamos pasado por alto sin tu informe.
teaching.explanationEs: Hit the nail on the head: hit no cambia en pasado; con he/she sería hits.
segments: You hit the nail on the head: that is exactly the
problem, and we would have missed it without your report.
teaching.audioText: You hit the nail on the head: that is exactly the problem, and we would have missed it without your report.

teaching.en: She has been under the weather all week, but she will weather the storm, and nobody will have to twist her arm to come to work on Monday.
teaching.es: Ha estado indispuesta toda la semana, pero superará el temporal, y nadie tendrá que torcerle el brazo para que venga a trabajar el lunes.
teaching.explanationEs: Under the weather es fija; solo cambia el tiempo de be (has been). Weather the storm: el verbo weather se conjuga.
segments: She has been under the weather all week, but she will weather the storm,
and nobody will have to twist her arm to come to work on Monday.
teaching.audioText: She has been under the weather all week, but she will weather the storm, and nobody will have to twist her arm to come to work on Monday.

teaching.en: Tom got cold feet the night before he signed, which cost the firm an arm and a leg in fees, but he hopes to find his feet in his next job.
teaching.es: Tom se echó atrás la noche antes de firmar, lo que le costó a la empresa un ojo de la cara en honorarios, pero espera adaptarse en su próximo empleo.
teaching.explanationEs: Get cold feet: get pasa a got y feet queda siempre en plural. Find your feet cambia el posesivo según la persona.
segments: Tom got cold feet the night before he signed, which cost the firm an arm and
a leg in fees, but he hopes to find his feet in his next job.
teaching.audioText: Tom got cold feet the night before he signed, which cost the firm an arm and a leg in fees, but he hopes to find his feet in his next job.

teaching.en: Only the verb changes: my sister always hits the nail on the head, but yesterday she spilled the beans about the trip.
teaching.es: Solo cambia el verbo: mi hermana siempre da en el clavo, pero ayer reveló el secreto del viaje.
teaching.explanationEs: Regla práctica: verbo flexible (hits, spilled), resto intacto (the nail on the head, the beans).
segments: Only the verb changes: my sister always hits the nail on
the head, but yesterday she spilled the beans about the trip.
teaching.audioText: Only the verb changes: my sister always hits the nail on the head, but yesterday she spilled the beans about the trip.

prompt.es: Completa: «Ayer Leo se armó de valor y llamó al dentista.»

answer.text: bit

feedback.es: El verbo del modismo va en pasado: bit, el pasado irregular de bite; the bullet no cambia.

hint.es: Es el pasado irregular de bite.

origin.text: Leo had avoided the dentist for months. Yesterday he finally ___ the bullet and called to book an appointment for Friday.

prompt.es: Elige la frase que cuenta lo ocurrido ayer con el modismo bien adaptado.

choices.text: Yesterday she spills the beans in the canteen.
Yesterday she has spilled the beans in the canteen.
Yesterday she spilled the beans in the canteen.

feedback.es: Con «yesterday» se usa el pasado simple: spilled. El presente o el present perfect no combinan con un momento terminado.

hint.es: Con «yesterday» hace falta el pasado simple.

origin.text: Mia had known about the surprise for a week, and she had promised Leo to keep quiet. Yet yesterday she told everyone in the canteen.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Mi hermana siempre da en el clavo.»

answer.text: My sister always hits the nail on the head

feedback.es: Con my sister (tercera persona) el verbo lleva -s: hits; la parte fija the nail on the head no cambia.

hint.es: Con my sister el verbo lleva -s.

prompt.es: Completa: «Esa cámara costó un ojo de la cara el año pasado.»

answer.text: cost

feedback.es: Cost es irregular: su pasado es cost, igual que el presente, y la parte fija an arm and a leg no cambia.

origin.text: I wanted the latest model, but it was far too expensive. That camera ___ an arm and a leg when it came out last year, so I bought a second-hand one.

prompt.es: Elige la frase que cuenta esto con el modismo bien adaptado al pasado.

choices.text: Yesterday Sara hit the nail on the head.
Yesterday Sara hit the nails on the head.
Yesterday Sara has hit the nail on the head.

feedback.es: Con «yesterday» va el pasado simple: hit, igual que el presente. Has hit no combina con un momento terminado, y the nail on the head no admite plural.

origin.text: In yesterday's meeting, Sara summed up the problem in one sentence, and everybody agreed that she had found exactly the right words.

prompt.es: Reescribe en pasado: «Mis padres se armaron de valor y vendieron el auto.»

answer.text: My parents bit the bullet and sold the car.
accepted: My parents bit the bullet and sold the car.
My parents bit the bullet and sold their car.

feedback.es: Los dos verbos pasan al pasado: bit (irregular) y sold (irregular); la parte fija the bullet no cambia.

origin.text: Family news: after years of delay, the decision was finally made. My parents bite the bullet and sell the car.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué actitud muestra Leo ante lo ocurrido.

choices.text: He is disappointed and will no longer trust Mia with any secrets.
He forgives her because the friendship matters more than the secret.
He is relieved that the whole class now knows about the trip.

feedback.es: Leo no se enfada: no quiere perder a una amiga por el secreto, aunque el viaje ya le costó mucho dinero.

origin.audio: Nobody was supposed to know about the trip to the coast. Leo had bought the tickets in secret, and Mia had promised to keep quiet. But on Monday, in the middle of a lesson, she spilled the beans, and by lunch the whole class was talking about the trip. Leo was not angry, though: he said the surprise had already cost an arm and a leg, and that he did not want to lose a friend over it as well.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Tom se echó atrás y nunca terminó el curso.»

answer.text: Tom got cold feet and never finished the course

feedback.es: Get pasa a got y cold feet queda intacto; never va antes del verbo finished.

prompt.es: Elige la frase que cuenta lo que hizo Carlos con el modismo bien adaptado.

choices.text: Yesterday Carlos bites the bullet and told his boss.
Yesterday Carlos bit the bullets and told his boss.
Yesterday Carlos bit the bullet and told his boss.

feedback.es: El verbo va en pasado (bit) y the bullet se mantiene en singular, como en la forma fija del modismo.

origin.text: Yesterday Carlos finally told his boss about the mistake. He had delayed it for weeks because he was afraid, but in the end he accepted the fear and did it.

prompt.es: Reescribe en pasado con «yesterday»: «Hoy me siento algo indispuesto.»

answer.text: Yesterday I felt under the weather.
accepted: Yesterday I felt under the weather.
Yesterday I was under the weather.
Yesterday I felt a little under the weather.
Yesterday I felt a bit under the weather.
Yesterday I was feeling under the weather.
I felt under the weather yesterday.
I was under the weather yesterday.

feedback.es: La parte fija under the weather se mantiene; solo cambia el verbo: felt o was.

origin.text: Message to a colleague: I am not well today, so I cannot join the call. Today I feel under the weather, but tomorrow I hope to be back.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué se puede deducir sobre la situación de Sara.

choices.text: She kept her job and is gradually feeling comfortable in it.
She narrowly kept her job but already finds the work too hard.
She plans to leave the company as soon as things improve.

feedback.es: Dodged a bullet indica que se libró de perder el empleo, y finding her feet, que se va adaptando poco a poco.

origin.audio: When the company lost its biggest client, nobody expected to keep their jobs. Somehow, everyone weathered the storm: the manager cut costs, the staff accepted shorter hours, and six months later things were stable. Sara, the newest worker, said that she had dodged a bullet, and that she was slowly finding her feet.

prompt.es: Completa: «Por favor, no reveles el secreto de mi sorpresa.»

answer.text: spill

feedback.es: Tras do not el verbo va en forma base: spill the beans; the beans no cambia.

origin.text: It is my sister's birthday on Saturday, and everything is ready. Please do not ___ the beans, or the whole plan will be ruined.

prompt.es: Ordena: «¿Costará el viaje un ojo de la cara este año?»

answer.text: Will the trip cost an arm and a leg this year

feedback.es: Con will el verbo queda en forma base: cost; la parte fija an arm and a leg no cambia.

es: Decidir si un modismo se usa en sentido literal o figurado en una conversación oída, apoyándote en una pista de contexto y en el tono.

vocabulary.es: literal, al pie de la letra
dar un paso adelante, asumir la responsabilidad

teaching.en: The boys broke the ice on the pond with a stick, so here the phrase is literal, and the clue is the frozen pond in front of them.
teaching.es: Los niños rompieron el hielo del estanque con un palo, así que aquí la expresión es literal, y la pista es el estanque helado que tienen delante.
teaching.explanationEs: Break the ice en sentido literal: hay hielo real en la escena; esa es la pista (clue).
segments: The boys broke the ice on the pond with a stick, so here the
phrase is literal, and the clue is the frozen pond in front of them.
teaching.audioText: The boys broke the ice on the pond with a stick, so here the phrase is literal, and the clue is the frozen pond in front of them.

teaching.en: I was nervous, so Mia told a joke to break the ice; the meaning is figurative because there was no ice anywhere near the table.
teaching.es: Estaba nervioso, así que Mia contó un chiste para romper el hielo; el sentido es figurado porque no había hielo cerca de la mesa.
teaching.explanationEs: Break the ice en sentido figurado: hacer que la gente se relaje al empezar una conversación.
segments: I was nervous, so Mia told a joke to break the ice; the
meaning is figurative because there was no ice anywhere near the table.
teaching.audioText: I was nervous, so Mia told a joke to break the ice; the meaning is figurative because there was no ice anywhere near the table.

teaching.en: After three mistakes in a week, Tom is on thin ice with his boss, and the clue is that the sentence is about work, not about a lake.
teaching.es: Tras tres errores en una semana, Tom está en la cuerda floja con su jefe, y la pista es que la frase habla de trabajo, no de un lago.
teaching.explanationEs: On thin ice: en riesgo de meterse en problemas; la pista es el jefe, no un lago.
segments: After three mistakes in a week, Tom is on thin ice with his boss,
and the clue is that the sentence is about work, not about a lake.
teaching.audioText: After three mistakes in a week, Tom is on thin ice with his boss, and the clue is that the sentence is about work, not about a lake.

teaching.en: I have a lot on my plate this week, so I cannot join you tonight; it is figurative, because nobody in the room is holding a plate.
teaching.es: Tengo mucho trabajo encima esta semana, así que no puedo unirme a ustedes esta noche; es figurado, porque nadie en la sala sostiene un plato.
teaching.explanationEs: A lot on my plate: mucho trabajo encima; sería literal solo con comida delante. Step up to the plate: asumir una responsabilidad.
segments: I have a lot on my plate this week, so I cannot join you
tonight; it is figurative, because nobody in the room is holding a plate.
teaching.audioText: I have a lot on my plate this week, so I cannot join you tonight; it is figurative, because nobody in the room is holding a plate.

teaching.en: If a friend asks whether you are pulling his leg, the tone is the clue: the phrase is figurative and means that you are joking.
teaching.es: Si un amigo te pregunta si le estás tomando el pelo, el tono es la pista: la frase es figurada y significa que bromeas.
teaching.explanationEs: Pull someone's leg: tomar el pelo, bromear; nadie toca ninguna pierna. El tono y la situación dan la pista.
segments: If a friend asks whether you are pulling his leg, the tone is
the clue: the phrase is figurative and means that you are joking.
teaching.audioText: If a friend asks whether you are pulling his leg, the tone is the clue: the phrase is figurative and means that you are joking.

teaching.en: He was very sarcastic when he said lovely weather in the storm; after an hour his jokes began to wear thin, so we decided to hit the road.
teaching.es: Fue muy sarcástico cuando dijo qué buen tiempo en plena tormenta; después de una hora sus bromas empezaron a cansar, así que decidimos ponernos en marcha.
teaching.explanationEs: Sarcasmo: dices lo contrario de lo que piensas. Wear thin: perder gracia. Hit the road: salir de viaje.
segments: He was very sarcastic when he said lovely weather in the storm; after an
hour his jokes began to wear thin, so we decided to hit the road.
teaching.audioText: He was very sarcastic when he said lovely weather in the storm; after an hour his jokes began to wear thin, so we decided to hit the road.

prompt.es: Decide si «break the ice» es literal o figurado en la escena.

choices.text: Literal: there is real ice on the pond in front of them.
Figurative: he asks the children to start a friendly conversation with him.
Figurative: he warns them that they are in serious trouble with him.

feedback.es: La pista es el estanque helado, el palo y el agua debajo: el hielo es real, así que la expresión es literal.

hint.es: Busca qué objeto real aparece en la escena.

origin.text: It was a freezing morning at the lake. Leo pointed at the pond and said to the little kids: “Careful! Do not break the ice with that stick; it is thin and the water below is deep.”

prompt.es: Completa: «Mia contó un chiste para romper el hielo y todos empezaron a hablar.»

answer.text: break

feedback.es: Break the ice, en sentido figurado, es hacer que la gente se relaje; aquí el chiste acaba con la incomodidad.

hint.es: Es el verbo que acompaña a ice en el modismo.

origin.text: Nobody at the table knew each other, and the silence was getting awkward. Finally Mia told a joke to ___ the ice, and within minutes everyone was talking.

prompt.es: Ordena: «¿Me estás tomando el pelo o es verdad?»

answer.text: Are you pulling my leg or is it true

feedback.es: Are you pulling my leg? es la pregunta fija para saber si alguien bromea; la parte fija es my leg.

hint.es: Empieza con Are you y sigue con pulling.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué significa «a lot on my plate» en esta conversación.

choices.text: Literal: she has too much food in front of her.
Figurative: she has too many tasks to attend dinner.
Figurative: she wants her friends to leave her alone.

feedback.es: Los informes, la reunión y la boda son la pista: «a lot on my plate» es figurado y significa tener muchas tareas.

origin.audio: Sorry, I cannot come tonight, Sara told her friends. I have a lot on my plate this week: two reports, a meeting with the client, and my brother's wedding on Saturday. Then she laughed and added that, if she skipped dinner as well, she would be on thin ice with her own mother. Her friends understood at once, because they know how busy her month has been. Two of them even offered to help with the reports, but she thanked them and said that some things she had to do herself.

prompt.es: Con la misma escena, ¿qué tono tiene la frase sobre su madre?

A sarcastic remark that means the opposite of what she says.
A playful joke that uses the idiom on purpose.

feedback.es: Sara se ríe y aplica «on thin ice» a su madre: es una broma que juega con el modismo, no una advertencia seria.

Amazing, Leo said with a big smile. Another meeting at seven. I love Mondays. Then he sat down and did not say a word for the rest of the day.

That she is very happy and wants to hear more details.

origin.audio: Hi team. I know many of you are new, so let me be careful with my words. We will hit the ground running on Monday. In other words, we start work at eight, and everybody needs to be ready with their task and their tools. On Friday we will touch base. In plain words, we meet for ten minutes to share our progress. I will keep my messages simple this week, and please tell me whenever something is not clear. See you there.

prompt.es: Elige la versión moderada del borrador con una alternativa clara.

origin.audio: Hello everyone. I need to apologise for the delay with the poster designs. I am afraid this is just the tip of the iceberg: the printer has also closed for the holidays, and two volunteers have dropped out. prompt.es: Escribe al equipo (unas 150 palabras): tres modismos y una alternativa sencilla.

answer.text: Hi team, the book fair starts on Monday, so we need to hit the ground running. In other words, we start work early and every person needs to know their task. Let's touch base on Friday for a short meeting to check our progress. I must also be honest: the delay with the posters is only the tip of the iceberg, because we still need more volunteers. In plain words, we have more problems than we thought, so please tell me if you can help. I do not want to use many idioms, so I will keep the rest simple. The plan is clear: posters on Tuesday, volunteers by Wednesday, and a last meeting on Friday. If any of you is not sure about a task, write to me tonight, and I will explain it in simple words. We are a small team, but I am sure that, working together, we can make this book fair a real success. Thank you for your work, and see you on Monday at eight!

Hello everyone, our book fair begins on Monday, so we have to hit the ground running. In other words, we start quickly and we all know our tasks. Let's touch base on Friday for a brief meeting. The delay with the posters is the tip of the iceberg, because we also need more volunteers. In plain words, there are more problems than we expected, so please tell me how you can help. I do not want to use many idioms, so I will keep the rest simple. The plan is clear: posters on Tuesday, volunteers by Wednesday, and a final meeting on Friday. Every person should know their task before Monday morning, and if something is not clear, please write to me tonight and I will explain it in simple words. To apologise for using an idiom that offended some of the visitors.

origin.audio: A colleague from abroad wrote to me: I read that our plan is on the back burner. Is something cooking? I smiled and answered in plain words: no, nobody is cooking. It means that we will work on the plan later, not now, because other tasks are more urgent this month.

prompt.es: Responde al mensaje de Sol: explica los dos modismos en inglés sencillo.

answer.text: Hi Sol, sorry about that. Those are idioms, and they do not mean what the words say. “Back to square one” means that we have to start again from the beginning. We made a plan, but it did not work, so we are at the start again. “Hit the nail on the head” means to say exactly the right thing. When Leo said the price was too high, he hit the nail on the head, because that was exactly the problem. In other words, the first idiom is about starting again and the second is about being exactly right. Let me put it simply: nobody is playing a game, and nobody is using a hammer. Does that make sense? If not, I can rephrase it or spell it out step by step. I will also write without idioms next time, so please tell me if any other phrase is unclear. I do not want anything to get lost in translation. Thank you for asking, and thanks for your patience!

Leo said the price was too high, and he was exactly right. In other words, the first idiom means we start again and the second means someone is correct. Is that clear? prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué opina Leo del comentario de Mia.

choices.text: He is slightly annoyed that she said aloud what he was about to say.
He agrees fully and likes the way she put it.
He is impressed but thinks she should have spoken before the meeting.

feedback.es: Leo dice que es exactamente lo que quería decir y que no encontraba las palabras: está de acuerdo y admira cómo lo dijo ella.

origin.audio: After the meeting, Leo said to Mia: you hit the nail on the head. That is exactly what I wanted to say, but I could not find the words. Mia laughed and answered that she had only said what everybody was thinking. Then a colleague from Brazil asked what the idiom meant, and Leo explained: it means that someone has said exactly the right thing.

prompt.es: Completa: «Déjame reformularlo: necesitamos tu respuesta para el viernes.»

feedback.es: Let me rephrase that es la fórmula para volver a decir lo mismo con otras palabras, más claras.

origin.text: I saw a confused look on her face after my long sentence, so I smiled and said: let me ___ that: we need your answer by Friday.

prompt.es: Elige la frase mejor escrita para un cliente extranjero.

choices.text: The offer is open, the ball is in your court and we are on the same page.
The offer is open; in a nutshell, it is a piece of cake to accept it.
The offer is open; in other words, you can accept it until Friday.

feedback.es: Es clara, da la fecha y usa in other words para simplificar; las otras acumulan modismos que el cliente dijo no entender.

origin.text: You are writing to a client who is learning English and who has told you that idioms are hard for him. You want to tell him that he can accept the offer until Friday.
